newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FEATURE - Austria's Hundertwasser ponders art, nature, socks.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Austria's Hundertwasser ponders art, nature, socks.

text.p: His golden onion domes, vibrant ceramic baubles and higgledy-piggledy houses make a curious sight among the cherubs and curlicues of Vienna's stately baroque architecture.

But Austrian painter and architect Friedensreich Hundertwasser claims to be an "architecture doctor, healing the soul-destroying environment of modern cities". His fundamental philosophy is: "The straight line is godless".

"I change sick houses into humane houses in harmony with nature," 68-year-old Hundertwasser told Reuters. "You cannot imagine how many people I have crying out to change the inhuman architecture everywhere."
Such statements have given Hundertwasser a reputation among some critics as a phoney, but there is no denying he has made his mark on architecture in this straight-laced country.
There is something joyfully childlike about the bulging forms of his art, which defy classical taste.
"The only way to get to your real self is to remember your childhood. Everything else is false," he says.

From an incinerator resembling a fairy castle in Vienna, to a colourful patchwork of council flats and a grass-roofed village complex in Blumau in East Styria, Hundertwasser's designs have become well-loved landmarks in Austria.
PUTTING NATURE IN THE HOME
Projects are also under way in Japan, the United States and Germany to put his ecological stamp on the landscape.
Hundertwasser brings nature back into the home by incorporating trees into the houses he designs. These "tree tenants", as he calls them, wave their branches from the windows like inhabitants.
Lanky, with a long beard, clogs and trademark odd socks, Hundertwasser looks exactly as one would imagine the architect of these lopsided unconventional creations.

"As an artist you have an obligation to respond to your visual world," he notes. Asked about his penchant for wearing odd socks, he said: "I always ask people why they wear the same two socks -- They are taught uniformity by society."

Hundertwasser, who has homes in New Zealand and Austria, was born Friedrich Stowasser in Vienna in 1928. His mother was Jewish and they spent the years of World War Two in hiding. He says 89 of his relatives were deported to concentration camps and never returned.
But he has not rejected his homeland.
Austria, birthplace of Adolf Hitler, is not particularly anti-Semitic, he says. "I see what happened as a very bad sickness that overcomes humanity from time to time," he explained.
"Austria is a very harsh place for sensitive artists, but its harshness creates a counter-reaction," he added.

As a painter Hundertwasser was strongly influenced by the post-World War Two abstract expressionist movement in Paris, including Rene Bro and Nicholas de Stael. It emphasised spontaneous expression of feeling rather than the geometric abstraction of followers of 20th century Dutch painter Piet Mondrian.

Hundertwasser's bright, vibrant canvases with titles like "Onion Tower Soup" appear to shrug off the fashionable gloom of much modern painting. "I want to make people feel that life is worth living," he says. "I hate hopeless art."
USE OF COLOUR EVOKES SUBCONSCIOUS
His paintings are often dominated by an enormous spiral and spattered by red, blue or silver droplets, a style that uses splashes of colour to evoke subconscious feelings.

Hundertwasser can devote hours to eulogising the spiral. "The spiral is the only organic form which is preliminary to life," he says. "It's the idea of renewal and deterioration, where life begins and ends."

His detractors see in his swirling curves and attention to minutiae a pale immitation of the late Viennese painter Gustav Klimt, a chief proponent of the turn-of-century Art Nouveau style. Hundertwasser, however, insists he is an original.
"I was one of the first to discover the dangers of the ruler in society," he says.
The maverick artist changed his name to Friedensreich Hundertwasser, meaning "Kingdom of peace Hundred waters" in German, to reflect his increasingly vocal ecological beliefs.
He has more than once created a stir by turning up naked in public to protest against what he calls "visual pollution", namely sterile architecture.
He also led an anti-European Union campaign in Austria, before its entry in 1995, claiming membership would be treason and likening the union to Nazi Germany, which annexed Austria in 1938.
Regarded as something of an eccentric for his outspoken stand against modern technology he says: "We're on the wrong track. Man should have nature as his master."

Critics of his work say Hundertwasser is overrated as an artist. "A picturesque figure given to gnomic utterances about his own significance in the world," was the appraisal given by the widely-read reference book "Who's Who".
Hundertwasser says he would like to be remembered "as a magician who finds a solution".
"It will take some time before people realise the dangers of the straight line," he predicts.
